description: We are a team of MCA batchmates from the Institute of Engineering and Technology (IET), Lucknow, with a shared interest in technology, coding and space exploration. We came together through the NASA Space Apps Challenge to combine our technical skills, creativity and problem-solving abilities to build CosmoCraft. As computer science students, we are excited to explore aerospace concepts, learn new technologies and create an engaging experience that makes space mission design accessible to all.
summary:
CosmoCraft is an interactive space mission simulator designed to make space exploration and spacecraft engineering easier and more interesting to learn. It gives users the opportunity to plan their own missions to Earth, the Moon, and Mars while making decisions about scientific instruments, spacecraft systems, communication, orbits, and launch vehicles.

Players can explore missions on their own or work together in teams, with each member taking responsibility for a different part of the mission. Along the way, they must balance factors such as mass, power, budget, and communication capacity to make their mission successful.

From designing the spacecraft to completing the flight readiness checks and watching the mission launch, every stage offers a hands-on way to understand the challenges behind real space missions. The simulator draws inspiration from NASA missions, technical references, and established scientific principles, bringing the engineering side of space exploration closer to students and space enthusiasts.
details:
About the Project

CosmoCraft is an interactive space mission design simulator that lets users experience what goes into planning and executing a space mission. The idea behind it is simple: instead of only reading about spacecraft engineering, users should be able to make mission decisions themselves, experiment with different configurations, and understand the challenges involved.

Users can choose missions to Earth, the Moon or Mars and play individually or collaborate in a team. Team Mode offers four specialized roles: Mission Planner, Systems Engineer, Science Lead and Telecommunications Officer. Each member contributes to a shared mission, making the experience more collaborative and engaging.

The main part of the experience is spacecraft engineering. Users select scientific instruments, configure power and communication systems, and monitor how their decisions affect parameters such as spacecraft mass, available power, budget and communication capacity. They then choose an orbit and launch vehicle before moving to the Flight Readiness Review, where the mission is checked against its engineering requirements.

Once the required checks are complete, the mission can be launched. A custom-built HTML5 Canvas animation brings the launch and mission sequence to life. After execution, users receive a mission report explaining the outcome and helping them understand the impact of their decisions. CosmoCraft also includes a Tutorial Academy to help beginners learn the concepts behind mission design.

NASA Relevance and Scientific Foundation

NASA missions and engineering references are an important part of CosmoCraft. The project's instrument catalogue includes technologies associated with missions such as Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, MAVEN and CALIPSO. Its spacecraft component catalogue draws inspiration from real technologies such as deployable solar arrays, radioisotope power systems and Deep Space Network communication systems.

The simulator also uses engineering references and scientific principles related to orbital Delta-V requirements, solar irradiance and deep-space communication losses. Its launch vehicle catalogue includes NASA's Space Launch System and other real-world launch vehicles.

These references help connect the experience to actual space exploration. The simulation simplifies complex engineering calculations for educational use and is not intended to replace professional mission-design software.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We want to make space science and aerospace engineering more approachable for students, beginners and anyone curious about space exploration. CosmoCraft provides a practical way to understand how scientific goals, engineering limitations and mission planning are connected.

It encourages users to think critically, experiment with different solutions, work together and learn from both successful and unsuccessful mission outcomes. It can be used as an introductory educational experience as well as an engaging way to explore the engineering behind space missions.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of CosmoCraft lies in bringing several stages of space mission planning into one connected experience. Scientific instrument selection, spacecraft configuration, communication, budgeting, launch planning and mission evaluation all influence one another.

The four-role collaboration system gives users different responsibilities, while the Flight Readiness Review introduces the importance of checking engineering requirements before launch. Rather than simply presenting information about space missions, CosmoCraft allows users to experience the decision-making process themselves.

The custom HTML5 Canvas-based animation system also provides an interactive visual representation of mission execution.

Technology Used

CosmoCraft is developed as a browser-based web application using React, TypeScript and Vite. Tailwind CSS is used for the interface, Zustand for application state management, and Firebase for authentication and real-time team collaboration. Structured JSON datasets organize mission information, instruments, spacecraft components, launch vehicles and orbital references.

The mission visuals and launch sequences are rendered through a custom HTML5 Canvas 2D engine. The application is designed to run in a modern web browser without requiring specialized hardware.

Factors Considered During Development

During development, we focused on making the experience understandable for beginners while retaining meaningful engineering concepts. We considered scientific relevance, usability, collaboration, visual clarity and the relationships between different spacecraft constraints.

We also aimed to keep the experience engaging without presenting simplified calculations as exact real-world mission predictions. Our goal was to create something that makes people curious about not just where space missions go, but how the engineering decisions behind them make those missions possible.
